note: Phosphorothioate nucleic acid polymers (REP 2055, REP 2139, REP 2165) that block HBsAg subviral-particle release went to patients on the DHBV Pekin-duck model; ducks and patients agreed, woodchuck and HBV-mouse models later failed to reproduce the effect, and HepG2.2.15 cells reproduced it.
label: Hep B (NAPs)

engagement.note: First peer-reviewed in-vivo use of a member: REP 2055 prevented DHBV infection in ducks at 1 mg/kg/day; serum DHBsAg is the read-out.
engagement.quote: A third NAP, REP 2055, which was designed to retain amphipathic activity at acidic pH and contained no CpG motifs, was well tolerated and displayed prophylactic activity against DHBV infection at doses as low as 1 mg/kg of body weight/day.
engagement.judgement: Opens the duck track at its first tier-1 in-vivo use for a member (REP 2055). The REP 101 patient trial had started in 2009 on earlier unpublished duck work, so by admissible sources the model precedes the patient data but the clinic ran in parallel; the therapeutic duck study is Noordeen 2015.

engagement.magnitude_basis: serum surface antigen: ducks cleared DHBsAg to undetectable with anti-DHBs appearance (Noordeen 2015); patients fell 2-7 log10 HBsAg with anti-HBs appearance; no shared number
engagement.confidence_note: Full text read (PMC4892580). The comparison is the sponsor's own. Retrodiction flag kept false because the duck therapeutic paper (Nov 2015) precedes the tier-1 patient paper (Jun 2016), but REP 101 ran 2009-2013 and the duck run dates are not given; Noordeen 2015 already claimed the patient replication as unpublished observation. Registry NCT02646163 posted retrospectively (2016-01-05) with no results.
engagement.note: REP 2055 cleared serum DHBsAg and raised anti-DHBs in ducks; in REP 101 patients REP 2055 monotherapy gave 2-7 log10 HBsAg reductions with anti-HBs appearance.
engagement.short: HBsAg fell 2-7 log as ducks predicted
engagement.quote: In both studies NAP monotherapy was accompanied by 2-7 log reductions of serum HBsAg, 3-9 log reductions in serum HBV DNA and the appearance of serum anti-HBsAg antibodies (10-1712 mIU / ml).
engagement.judgement: Stated comparison: the trial paper's introduction and discussion set the duck DHBsAg clearance beside the patient HBsAg decline (REP 2055 'resulted in the rapid clearance of duck HBsAg' then 'substantial reductions in serum HBsAg'). Serum HBsAg is the product of the blocked process (subviral-particle release), so readout_tier proximal. Direction only: the duck abstract gives no log reduction.

engagement.magnitude_basis: REP 2165 vs REP 2139 antiviral activity: similar in ducks, no significant difference in HBsAg, anti-HBs or HBV DNA in REP 401 patients
engagement.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading of Bazinet 2020 (Gastroenterology, no PMC copy); Roehl 2017 full text read (PMC5466589). Pairing is mine: the trial abstract does not cite the duck data. NCT02565719 has no posted results (primary outcome: adverse events).
engagement.note: Ducks predicted REP 2165 would match REP 2139 (Roehl 2017); in REP 401, HBsAg, anti-HBs and HBV DNA did not differ between arms.
engagement.short: REP 2165 matched REP 2139 as ducks predicted
engagement.quote: Levels of HBsAg, anti-HBs, and HBV DNA did not differ significantly between the groups given REP 2139 vs REP 2165.
engagement.reason: Duck HBsAg read-out held for all three members
engagement.judgement: Second prospective duck prediction on the same track, so strengthens rather than a status change: Roehl 2017 stated 'the therapeutic potential of REP 2165 against chronic HBV infection in patients is similar to REP 2139' from DHBV ducks, and the randomised REP 2139 vs REP 2165 arms agreed. Both are members, product_in_model true.

engagement.magnitude_basis: serum surface antigen reduction: 36-79% (under 1 log10) in 4/10 woodchucks, no WHV DNA change, vs 2-7 log10 HBsAg and 3-9 log10 HBV DNA in patients
engagement.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading (Europe PMC full text not available). Experiment dates are not given; scored as a retrodiction because the paper (Nov 2017) frames the models against patient results already published (Al-Mahtab 2016). Status is contra either way.
engagement.note: REP 2139 in WHV-infected woodchucks gave mild WHsAg reductions in 4/10 and no WHV DNA change, against multilog HBsAg loss in patients.
engagement.short: Woodchucks miss the patient HBsAg response
engagement.quote: However, in woodchucks, NAP treatment was associated with only mild (36-79% relative to baseline) reductions in WHsAg (4/10 animals) after 3-5 weeks of treatment without changes in serum WHV DNA.
engagement.reason: Failed to reproduce the patient HBsAg loss
engagement.judgement: Retrodiction that failed to reproduce the human data, so contra (decision 10). The source states the comparison itself: 'the antiviral effects of NAPs in DHBV infected ducks and patients with chronic HBV infection were weak or absent in woodchuck and mouse models'. Separate track from the mouse systems per the identity rule (different species and virus). First use of this model for the class is the comparison itself, so no untested opener.

engagement.magnitude_basis: serum HBsAg reduction: none in HBV-transgenic mice over 12 weeks of REP 2139 vs 2-7 log10 in patients
engagement.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading. Experiment dates not given; retrodiction inferred from publication after Al-Mahtab 2016 and the paper's own framing against patient results.
engagement.note: REP 2139 for up to 12 weeks lowered no serum HBsAg in HBV-transgenic mice, set against the multilog HBsAg loss already seen in patients.
engagement.short: Transgenic mice show no HBsAg fall
engagement.quote: In HBV transgenic mice, no reductions in serum HBsAg were observed with REP 2139 with up to 12 weeks of treatment.
engagement.reason: Failed to reproduce the patient HBsAg loss
engagement.judgement: Retrodiction that failed, so contra. The paper attributes the miss to rodent subviral-particle assembly or secretion differing from DHBV and human infection, which is a model-validity verdict, not a drug failure. Own track per the identity rule; the siRNA tile's hbv-genome-mouse is a different construct (transient/AAV) and is not reused.

engagement.magnitude_basis: serum HBsAg, HBeAg and HBV DNA: no reduction after 28 days of REP 2055 in HBV-infected SCID-Hu mice vs 2-7 log10 HBsAg in REP 2055 patients
engagement.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading. Experiment dates not given; retrodiction inferred from publication after Al-Mahtab 2016. Same slug as the siRNA tile's human-liver-chimeric mouse because it is the same system (human hepatocytes in immunodeficient mice).
engagement.note: REP 2055, the member that cleared HBsAg in REP 101 patients, moved no HBsAg, HBeAg or HBV DNA in HBV-infected SCID-Hu mice over 28 days.
engagement.short: Chimeric mice show no HBsAg fall
engagement.quote: In HBV infected SCID-Hu mice, REP 2055 treatment was not associated with any reduction of HBsAg, HBeAg or HBV DNA in the serum after 28 days of treatment.
engagement.reason: Failed to reproduce the patient HBsAg loss
engagement.judgement: Retrodiction that failed, so contra. Striking because the hepatocytes are human: the paper notes liver NAP accumulation was similar across species, so the miss is not delivery. Kept apart from the transgenic mouse and the woodchuck per the identity rule.

engagement.magnitude_basis: HBsAg secretion inhibition in vitro vs serum HBsAg clearance in patients; no shared quantity
engagement.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading (paywalled). model_kind ex_vivo because the enum has no in-vitro value; HepG2.2.15 is a hepatoma line. The assay needs the endosomal-release compound UNC7938 to work, which the patients did not receive.
engagement.model: HepG2.2.15 HBsAg-secretion assay (with UNC7938 endosomal release)
engagement.note: Built after the clinic: HepG2.2.15 cells with UNC7938 recapitulated the selective block of HBsAg secretion that NAPs had already shown in patients.
engagement.short: Cells reproduce the patient HBsAg block
engagement.quote: In this study, we show for the first time the recapitulation of NAP- induced inhibition of secretion of HBsAg in vitro using the human HepG2.2.15 cell line.
engagement.reason: Built after the clinic; reproduces the HBsAg block
engagement.judgement: Retrodiction by the source's own words ('recapitulation'); Boulon 2020 (doi 10.1016/j.antiviral.2020.104853) repeats it for REP 2139: 'This assay recapitulates the HBsAg secretion inhibition observed in treated patients.' Retro, never same (decision 10). No prospective patient prediction from this track has been tested.

engagement.magnitude_basis: responder fraction: about half of REP 2139-treated ducks vs a subset of REP 401 patients (24/40 HBsAg loss on therapy); REP 2165 differed in ducks but not in patients
engagement.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading (paywalled). Separate track from the Replicor/Adelaide duck: a re-engineered system (subcutaneous dosing, experimentally infected adult ducks, Aligos) built after REP 401 reported, with a different prediction (responder/non-responder split, REP 2165 faster rebound).
engagement.model: Optimised DHBV duck model (Aligos, subcutaneous NAP dosing)
engagement.note: A competitor's optimised duck model, built after REP 401, reproduced the patient responder split but gave REP 2165 a profile patients did not show.
engagement.quote: It recapitulates many aspects of this class of compound's efficacy in CHB patients, most notably the clear division between responders and non-responders.
engagement.reason: Built after the clinic; partial reproduction
engagement.judgement: Retrodiction (decision 10): the source says 'recapitulates' and names patient outcomes. Partial because the abstract gives REP 2165 'a more homogenous antiviral response followed by a faster rebound', whereas REP 401 found no REP 2139 vs REP 2165 difference, and efficacy appeared only in experimentally infected, not vertically infected, ducks.

engagement.confidence_note: Full text read (PMC5479567, open access; PLoS JATS XML checked). model_kind ex_vivo because the enum has no in-vitro value: PHH are primary human cells, HepaRG a differentiated human hepatoma line. Opener and comparison share a year because the first use of this system for the class is the comparison paper.
engagement.model: HBV-infected HepaRG cells and primary human hepatocytes (NAP at or after inoculation)
engagement.note: First human-cell use of the class: REP 2055, REP 2139 and REP 2165 added at or after HBV inoculation of HepaRG and PHH; HBsAg, HBeAg and HBV RNA read out.
engagement.short: NAPs tested in HepaRG and human hepatocytes
engagement.quote: In this study, we investigated the specific anti-HBV antiviral activity of NAPs in the HepaRG human hepatoma cell line and primary cultures of human hepatocytes.
engagement.judgement: Opens the human-cell track at its first admissible use (epub 2017-06-21). Separate track from the draft's HepG2.2.15/UNC7938 assay (Blanchet 2019): different cells, HBV infection rather than an integrated genome, no endosomal-release agent, and the opposite prediction. Separate from the duck primary-hepatocyte assay (different species and virus).

engagement.magnitude_basis: post-inoculation HBsAg secretion: no change in HepaRG or PHH at up to 5 uM REP 2055 or REP 2139 ('did not elicit any antiviral activity'), vs 2-7 log10 serum HBsAg decline in REP 101/REP 102 patients (Al-Mahtab 2016); and REP 2055 blocked entry much more efficiently than REP 2139 while the two were comparable in patients
engagement.confidence_note: Full text read (PMC5479567); the quote was checked against the PLoS JATS XML so the italic 'in vitro' is in place. The patient side is the sponsor's open-label REP 101/REP 102 series (Al-Mahtab 2016), cited by the source. The source attributes the post-entry failure to endosomal sequestration of naked oligonucleotides in culture, which Blanchet 2019 later bypassed with UNC7938 (the draft's hepg2215-hbsag-secretion track).
engagement.model: HBV-infected HepaRG cells and primary human hepatocytes (NAP at or after inoculation)
engagement.note: Human hepatocyte cultures blocked HBV entry but showed no post-inoculation effect on HBsAg and ranked REP 2055 far above REP 2139, against the comparable multilog HBsAg loss both gave patients.
engagement.short: Human hepatocytes miss the patient HBsAg block
engagement.quote: Importantly, the in vitro data presented here show that REP 2055 blocks HBV entry much more efficiently than REP 2139, while the antiviral activity for these two compounds is comparable in proof of concept clinical trials
engagement.reason: Failed to reproduce the patient HBsAg loss
engagement.judgement: Retrodiction: the paper opens from the patient HBsAg clearance already published (Al-Mahtab 2016) and sets its own results against the proof-of-concept trials in two places (Results: 'While exhibiting a similar antiviral activity in proof of concept clinical trials, the in vitro ability of REP 2139 ... was significantly reduced as compared to REP 2055'; Discussion as quoted), so comparison_stated true. It failed on both counts the patients could test: no post-entry HBsAg effect in infected cells ('NAP treatment after viral inoculation did not elicit any antiviral activity', abstract) where patients lose 2-7 log10 HBsAg, and a REP 2055 >> REP 2139 entry ranking where the clinic saw comparable activity. A failed retrodiction is contra, never retro (decision 10). The entry block it did show has no patient counterpart (no prophylaxis trial), so it earns nothing. Only engagement is scored: the assay predicts nothing about off-treatment control (efficacy), exposure (dose) or harm (safety; neutral-red cytotoxicity only, no patient comparison stated). A failed model stays failed on its track; no later prospective prediction from this system has been tested.

dose.note: Ducks got 2-10 mg/kg/day, and weekly dosing copied from human PS-ON practice; the duck set no human exposure target.
dose.short: Ducks copied the human regimen; no target
dose.quote: In all REP 2055-treated ducks, 28 days of treatment lead to initial rapid reductions in serum DHBsAg and DHBV DNA and increases in anti-DHBs antibodies.
dose.reason: No human exposure target stated by the duck
dose.judgement: The duck opener is 2015, not 2013, because the 2013 prophylaxis study carried no therapeutic regimen. Patients in REP 101 received REP 2055 at 400-1200 mg intravenously (Al-Mahtab 2016 full text) while ducks got 10 mg/kg intraperitoneally; no source maps one onto the other, so a drafter-made mg/kg mapping is not scored. The tolerated-dose margin is scored on the toxicology-species track.

dose.confidence_note: Full text read (PMC5466589, open access): cynomolgus monkeys tolerated 6 months at up to 9 mg/kg with no change in body weight gain, liver or kidney function, calcium homeostasis or haematology; at 27 mg/kg females gained less weight.
dose.note: REP 2139 and REP 2165 tolerated in mice and cynomolgus at clinically relevant doses (9 mg/kg, 6 months) with no liver, kidney or haematological change.
dose.quote: Both REP 2139 and REP 2165 were well tolerated at clinically relevant doses, with no alterations in liver, kidney, or hematological function.
dose.judgement: Opens the toxicology-species track: the first tier-1 statement of a tolerated exposure at or above the effective one (ducks were effective at 10 mg/kg three times weekly in the same paper). Published while REP 401 was enrolling (start 2016-03), so prospective for the REP 401 read-out.

dose.magnitude_basis: tolerated-dose margin: monkey 9 mg/kg for 6 months vs patient 250 mg (about 3.5 mg/kg) weekly for 48 weeks; no shared efficacy exposure
dose.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading of Bazinet 2020; the pairing with Roehl 2017 is mine. Whether REP 401 patients received mineral supplementation, as REP 101 patients did after hypocalcaemia at 400 mg REP 2055, was not verified.
dose.note: REP 401 dosed REP 2139-Mg or REP 2165-Mg at 250 mg weekly, inside the monkey margin, tolerability unaltered; HBsAg fell to 0.05 IU/mL in 24/40.
dose.short: Dosed inside the margin; HBsAg lost in 24/40
dose.quote: At the time patients completed the TDF + pegIFN + NAP regimen, HBsAg levels were 0.05 IU/mL or lower in 24/40 participants (all with seroconversion up to 233,055 mIU/mL).
dose.reason: Tolerated margin held; drug worked at target
dose.judgement: Decision 16: the model stated the effective exposure was tolerated (no liver, kidney, calcium or haematological change at up to 9 mg/kg) and patients were dosed to a clinically relevant weekly dose without that toxicity while the drug worked, so same with margin_stated true. The NAP-arm transaminase rises are scored in safety, not here, because they tracked HBsAg loss rather than exposure.

efficacy.note: Immunocompetent ducks with persistent DHBV can express off-treatment control (DHBsAg loss, anti-DHBs, liver cccDNA), the class's functional-cure endpoint; 2013 work was prophylaxis only.
efficacy.quote: A third NAP, REP 2055, which was designed to retain amphipathic activity at acidic pH and contained no CpG motifs, was well tolerated and displayed prophylactic activity against DHBV infection at doses as low as 1 mg/kg of body weight/day.
efficacy.judgement: Opener for the duck track; the therapeutic prediction (sustained virologic response in 6/11 ducks after 28 days of REP 2055) is Noordeen 2015 and is the model side of the 2016 comparison.

efficacy.magnitude_basis: fraction with sustained off-treatment control after NAP monotherapy: 6/11 ducks (55%) at 9-16 weeks vs 3/8 REP 2055 patients (38%) without rebound at 52 weeks
efficacy.confidence_note: Full text read (PMC4892580). Sponsor-authored, open-label, n=8; the registry primary outcome is safety and tolerability, so the efficacy outcome is the sponsor's proof-of-concept gate. Retrodiction caveat as in engagement: REP 101 ran 2009-2013, the duck therapeutic run dates are not given.
efficacy.note: Ducks predicted sustained off-treatment control in a subset (6/11); in REP 101, 3/8 REP 2055 patients stayed without rebound for 52 weeks.
efficacy.short: 3/8 patients in sustained control, as 6/11 ducks
efficacy.quote: For 52 weeks after removal of REP 2055 therapy, rebound of serum viremia (HBV DNA > 1000 copies / ml, HBsAg > 1IU / ml) was not observed in 3 / 8 patients.
efficacy.reason: Off-treatment control in a subset, as in ducks
efficacy.judgement: Stated comparison: the trial paper's discussion sets the duck therapeutic outcome beside the patient data. Scored on the proof-of-concept gate because the registry primary (NCT02646163, posted retrospectively 2016-01-05, no results) is safety. Later member trials are listed in patient_trials and change no status: REP 301 and REP 401 added pegIFN, so the duck's untested prediction that REP 2139 plus a nucleos(t)ide alone controls infection without pegIFN (Quinet 2018, doi 10.1002/hep.29737) remains untested. The woodchuck and mouse models in the engagement cell predicted no antiviral effect at all and are not re-scored here.

patient_trials.quote: Six patients had HBsAg levels less than 50 IU/mL by the end of treatment (all <0·05 IU/mL); five maintained this level of suppression at the end of 1 year follow-up.

During 48 weeks of treatment-free follow-up, virologic control persisted in 13 of 40 participants (2 lost to follow-up after 24 weeks), whereas functional cure persisted in 14 of 40 participants (all completing 48 weeks of follow-up) with persistent HBsAg seroconversion.
HDV functional cure persisted in 7 of 11 participants; HBV virologic control persisted in 3 and functional cure (with HBsAg seroconversion) persisted in 4 of these participants.

safety.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading of Noordeen 2013; Noordeen 2015 full text reports tolerability as body weight only (plus procedure-related peritoneal abscesses from repeated intraperitoneal injection).
safety.note: Ducks flagged the CpG NAP REP 2006 as toxic and REP 2055 as well tolerated, on body weight; no source compares duck tolerability with patients.
safety.short: Ducks: CpG NAP toxic, REP 2055 tolerated
safety.quote: REP 2006 displayed significant toxicity in ducks, which was attributed to CpG-mediated proinflammation, while REP 2031 (which has no CpG motifs) displayed no toxicity.
safety.judgement: Left untested rather than scored: REP 101/102 patients had infusion-related 'administration tolerability issues', gum bleeding with raised INR at 1200 mg, asymptomatic hypocalcaemia at 400 mg, and hair loss, dysphagia and dysgeusia on REP 2139-Ca that the sponsor attributes to heavy-metal exposure endemic at the Bangladesh site (Al-Mahtab 2016). Ducks measured neither calcium nor coagulation and received intraperitoneal bolus doses, and no source puts duck and patient tolerability side by side; the explicit tolerability margin is on the toxicology-species track.

safety.confidence_note: Full text read (PMC5466589). The paper also discusses phosphorothioate mineral chelation and the Bangladesh heavy-metal symptoms, and reports calcium homeostasis unchanged in monkeys at up to 9 mg/kg.
safety.note: Six-month cynomolgus toxicology: no liver, kidney, calcium or haematological change at up to 9 mg/kg, the stated prediction for patients.
safety.quote: Both REP 2139 and REP 2165 were well tolerated at clinically relevant doses, with no alterations in liver, kidney, or hematological function.
safety.judgement: Opens the toxicology-species track at its first tier-1 report; the earlier Bangladesh harms (2016) predate this prediction and are recorded on the duck opener.

safety.magnitude_basis: tolerability: no liver, kidney or haematological change in monkeys vs unaltered tolerability and pegIFN cytopenias unaffected by NAPs in REP 401; transaminase rises in NAP arms were asymptomatic and tracked HBsAg loss
safety.confidence_note: Abstract-level reading of Bazinet 2020; pairing with Roehl 2017 is mine. Open-label n=40, HBeAg-negative patients on TDF plus pegIFN background. Bazinet 2021 (doi 10.1111/jvh.13483) reports transaminase elevations in 95% of REP 401 participants, asymptomatic and predictive of functional cure.
safety.note: NAPs added to TDF plus pegIFN did not alter tolerability or cytopenias; transaminase rises were asymptomatic and tied to HBsAg loss.
safety.short: Tolerability unaltered; flares tracked HBsAg loss
safety.quote: In a phase 2 randomized trial, we found that addition of NAPs to TDF + pegIFN did not alter tolerability and significantly increased rates of HBsAg loss and HBsAg seroconversion during therapy and functional cure after therapy.
safety.reason: Monkey tolerability held; immune flares not a miss
safety.judgement: The stated prediction (no liver, kidney or haematological harm at clinically relevant doses) held for the drug's own toxicity: NAPs did not change tolerability or pegIFN cytopenias. The NAP-arm transaminase elevations (P < .001 vs controls) are host-mediated flares that accompany HBsAg clearance in infected patients; an uninfected cynomolgus cannot show them, so the silence is not a miss and the entry is same with source_calls_it partial. The Bangladesh heavy-metal symptoms and hypocalcaemia on REP 2055 (2016) predate this prediction and did not recur in the Moldova trials (REP 301-LTF: no long-term safety issues, Bazinet 2021).

safety.confidence_note: Full text read (PMC5341074 via Europe PMC; published 2017-03-08). Liver cells from surgical resections, PBMC from healthy volunteers; REP 2006, REP 2055, REP 2139 and REP 2165 at 0.05-50 uM; qRT-PCR and ELISA for TNF, IL6, IL10 and interferon genes against TLR3/7/8/9 agonist controls. model_kind ex_vivo (human primary cells).
safety.model: Primary human hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells and PBMC cytokine-induction assay (uninfected)
safety.note: All three members dosed on human liver cells and PBMC: no inflammatory or interferon response in hepatocytes or LSEC; weak TNF/IL6 in Kupffer cells and PBMC, secretion only at 50 uM.
safety.short: Human liver cells: NAPs barely immunostimulatory
safety.quote: In primary isolated human hepatocytes and liver sinusoidal endothelial cells no significant inflammatory or antiviral responses were detected for any NAPs.
safety.judgement: Opens a human ex-vivo immune track for the platform harm of phosphorothioate oligonucleotides (innate immunostimulation), which these cells, unlike the draft's mouse and cynomolgus toxicology, can show directly. Separate track from heparg-phh-hbv-entry: uninfected cells, an immune readout and a different prediction. Opener and comparison share a year because the first use is the comparison paper.

safety.magnitude_basis: cytokine induction: weak TNF/IL6 only in Kupffer cells and PBMC, no interferon response, secretion only at 50 uM (about 5x cynomolgus Cmax) in the model, vs serum cytokine elevations in all REP 102 patients at therapeutic doses that did not track HBsAg decline, with no pro-inflammatory clinical effects reported (Al-Mahtab 2016)
safety.confidence_note: Full text read (PMC5341074). The patient-side cytokine data the source cites are an EASL 2015 abstract (Stelma et al., J Hepatol 62:S567), not a peer-reviewed paper; the comparison is admissible only because the tier-1 source states it. Replicor-coauthored. The status is a judgement call: read at the biomarker level (cytokines rose in all patients where the cells said therapeutic exposure was too low) it is contra; read at the harm level (no pro-inflammatory clinical effect, as the cells predicted) it is retro. Scored retro + partial for consistency with the draft's cynomolgus safety entry, where host-immune events in infected patients that an uninfected system cannot show were not counted as a miss. Registry: REP 102 is NCT02646189 (first posted 2016-01-05, start 2011-08, no results posted; NCT02726789, start 2012-10, results 2019-05-08, is a second REP 2139-Ca + pegIFN Bangladeshi record and may also be REP 102); the comparison itself became public with the paper, so year stays 2017.
safety.model: Primary human hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells and PBMC cytokine-induction assay (uninfected)
safety.note: Built after the clinic: weak, supra-therapeutic-only cytokine induction in human liver cells and PBMC, set against REP 102 serum cytokine rises that did not track HBsAg loss and no clinical pro-inflammatory effects.
safety.short: Human cells reproduce weak immunostimulation, partly
safety.quote: Indeed, elevation of serum cytokines are observed in all patients receiving REP 2139 in the REP 102 protocol but these elevations are not correlated with a reduction in serum HBsAg.
safety.reason: Weak immunostimulation reproduced; cytokine rise under-called
safety.judgement: Retrodiction: the paper takes the patient HBsAg clearance (Al-Mahtab 2016) and the REP 102 cytokine data (Stelma 2015) as known and sets its cells beside them in its own words ('persist and are not accompanied by pro-inflammatory effects in vivo or in human patients'; 'well before any immunostimulatory or pro-inflammatory activity would be predicted to occur based on pharmacokinetics in non-human primates and the weak pro-inflammatory and immunostimulatory properties of NAPs observed in this study'), so comparison_stated true. What the cells reproduced: weak pro-inflammatory (TNF, IL6) and no interferon induction, matching the absence of NAP-attributable pro-inflammatory harm in REP 101/102 and later REP 401 (Bazinet 2020, 'did not alter tolerability'). What they under-called: the exposure threshold (secretion only at 50 uM) against serum cytokine elevations in all REP 102 patients at therapeutic doses; the source resolves this by uncorrelation with HBsAg decline, a mechanism argument, so partial. Retro, never same (decision 10). Safety, not engagement: the readout is the platform harm of PS-oligonucleotides, not the class PD (HBsAg). No prospective prediction from this track has been tested since.
